analysis_steps.goal: Decompose low-frequency radio spectra to measure extended 300-MHz luminosity, 1.4-GHz core luminosity, core dominance, and crossing frequency

method.value: Compare single and added power-law fits to data below 10^13 Hz using a chi-squared test (2 dof, significance > 0.95), or fit/extrapolate direct extended flux measurements from radio maps to 300 MHz.

evidence.quote: For each source, we initially took all data below $10^{13}$ Hz and compared single and added power-law fits to the data. As these are nested models, with the added power law having two additional degrees of freedom (the normalization and index of the second power law), a $\chi^2$ test with 2 degrees of freedom was used.
The 300-MHz flux can then be estimated either through a fit to two or more extended flux measurements or by extrapolating from a single point to 300 MHz with a spectral index of 0.7 (e.g., M11).

findings_qualitative.value: There is little evidence for the blazar sequence anti-correlation; the 'forbidden zone' at high peak frequency and high peak luminosity is populated by highly aligned type I BL Lacs.

evidence.quote: Here, based on the largest-ever sample of over 2000 well-sampled jet spectral energy distributions, we examine the synchrotron peak frequency – peak luminosity plane, and find little evidence for the anti-correlation known as the blazar sequence.

We find that there is no ‘forbidden zone’ at high-$\nu_\mathrm{peak}$ and high $L_\mathrm{peak}$, but rather that this area of the plane is populated by type I ("weak" or inefficiently accreting) BL Lacs.

findings_qualitative.value: Jetted AGN exhibit a dichotomy between type II (strong, efficient accretion) and type I (weak, inefficient accretion) jets, which is not a simple division in jet power.

evidence.quote: Instead, we find strong evidence for a dichotomy in jets, between those associated with efficient or ‘quasar-mode’ accretion (strong/type II jets) and those associated with inefficient accretion (weak/type I jets).
We have derived estimates of the total jet power for over 1000 of our sources from low-frequency radio observations, and find that the jet dichotomy does *not* correspond to a division in jet power.

findings_qualitative.value: Low-synchrotron-peak BL Lacs (LBLs) in the strong zone have extended radio power distributions, big blue bump signatures, and hotspots consistent with FSRQs and should be classified as type II jets.

evidence.quote: It is clear that the mean and distribution of $L_\mathrm{ext}$ for strong-zone BLLs is far more similar to FSRQ than to the high-$\nu_\mathrm{peak}$, weak-zone BLLs. Given these observations, as well as the fact that many LBLs have extended radio powers well above what are observed for FR I radio galaxies (cite: rector01), it seems that LBLs should be classified as type II jets along with FSRQ.

claims.hypothesis: The synchrotron peak luminosity and peak frequency of blazars follow a monoparametric anti-correlation driven by jet power (the blazar sequence), leaving a forbidden zone at high peak frequency and high peak luminosity.
claims.experiment: Compiled 2124 well-sampled jet SEDs (1045 TEX with measured 300-MHz extended radio luminosity and 1079 UEX with upper limits) and examined their distribution in the nu_peak - L_peak plane across bins of L_ext.
claims.result: Found 30 sources in the high-nu_peak (>10^15 Hz), high-L_peak (>10^46 erg/s) zone, and found that type II jets have a constant average nu_peak (~10^13.3 Hz) across 4 orders of magnitude in jet power.
claims.finding: The blazar sequence anti-correlation is not supported; jets are not monoparametric and there is no forbidden zone at high peak frequency and high peak luminosity.

evidence.loc: The End of the Blazar Sequence
evidence.quote: In the combined sample there are 30 sources with $\nu_\mathrm{peak} > 10^{15}$ Hz and $L_\mathrm{peak} > 10^46$ erg/s while in the TEX there are only 11.

evidence.loc: The End of the Blazar Sequence
evidence.quote: As shown in Figure 2, we see that type II jets have a remarkably consistent distribution of synchroton peak frequencies over 4 orders of magnitude in jet power, as every bin has an average value of approximately $\nu_\mathrm{peak} = 10^{13.3}$ Hz

One of the main attractions of the blazar sequence paradigm was the idea that jets might be monoparametric, with their spectral type and broad SED characteristics predicted by a single parameter, the jet power. However we have shown that outside of the extreme high-power tail of the population, this is not the case.

claims.hypothesis: Relativistic jets divide into two distinct classes (type I/weak and type II/strong) driven by accretion mode (inefficient vs. efficient) rather than a simple threshold in total jet power.
claims.experiment: Compared extended 300-MHz radio power (L_ext), black hole masses (M_BH), and Eddington ratios (log L_kin/L_edd) between strong-zone (type II) and weak-zone (type I) sources.
claims.result: Type II jets span over 4 decades in L_ext down to <10^41 erg/s with nu_peak < 10^15 Hz, whereas type I jets have an upper bound at L_ext ~ 10^43 erg/s (matching ~0.5-5% Eddington for 10^9.5 M_sun black holes) and divide from type II at log(L_kin/L_edd) ~ -2.5.
claims.finding: The jet dichotomy corresponds to efficient vs. inefficient accretion onto black holes of similar mass distributions (10^7 - 10^9.5 M_sun), explaining both the overlap in jet power and the upper bound on type I jet power.

evidence.quote: Rather, type II jets are produced at *all* observed jet powers, down to the lowest levels in our sample, while type I jets range from very low to moderately high jet powers, with a clear upper bound at $\sim10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$.

evidence.loc: Accretion Mode in type I and II Jets
evidence.quote: In agreement with previous work, we see a divide in Eddington ratio at $L_\textrm{kin}/L_\textrm{edd}\approx-2.5$.

claims.hypothesis: Low-synchrotron-peak BL Lacs (LBLs) in the strong zone are actually type II jets (misidentified FSRQs whose broad lines are swamped by beamed jet emission).
claims.experiment: Examined the locations of BL Lacs with big blue bump (BBB) accretion disk signatures or VLA hotspots in the nu_peak - L_peak plane and compared the L_ext distribution of strong-zone BLLs to FSRQs and weak-zone BLLs.
claims.result: Essentially all BL Lacs with a BBB signature or hotspot lie in the strong zone (nu_peak < 10^15 Hz), and the L_ext distribution of strong-zone BLLs closely matches that of FSRQs rather than high-nu_peak BLLs.
claims.finding: LBLs are predominantly type II jets and should be grouped with FSRQs and FR IIs rather than HBLs.

evidence.quote: Essentially *all* the BL Lacs with either a BBB signature or a hotspot occur in the same zone which contains essentially all the broad-lined blazars (e.g., the boxed area which has a maximum $\nu_\mathrm{peak}$ value of $10^{15}$ Hz).

It is clear that the mean and distribution of $L_\mathrm{ext}$ for strong-zone BLLs is far more similar to FSRQ than to the high-$\nu_\mathrm{peak}$, weak-zone BLLs. Given these observations, as well as the fact that many LBLs have extended radio powers well above what are observed for FR I radio galaxies (cite: rector01), it seems that LBLs should be classified as type II jets along with FSRQ.

claims.hypothesis: Type I jets possess velocity gradients (structured/decelerating flows) that cause them to follow horizontal de-beaming tracks in the nu_peak - L_peak plane as viewing angle increases.
claims.experiment: Compared the distribution of sources, an empirical Orientation Indicator (OI), and VLBI apparent jet speeds (beta_app) in the nu_peak - L_peak plane against theoretical de-beaming tracks for single-velocity versus decelerating flows.
claims.result: Decelerating flow tracks with Gamma_init = 6-26 and Gamma_fin = 3 reproduce the spread of weak-zone blazars and the dearth of high-nu_peak, low-L_peak radio galaxies, while OI and beta_app maps show lower speeds and increasing misalignment toward lower L_peak and lower nu_peak.
claims.finding: Observational trends in the nu_peak - L_peak plane support velocity gradients in type I jets and largely horizontal de-beaming paths.

evidence.loc: Velocity Gradients in Type I Jets
evidence.quote: As shown, a simple jet model with velocity gradients allows us to explain the wide range of peak frequencies and luminosities of blazars in the weak-jet region with very reasonable values of $\Gamma$, while remaining consistent with the location of misaligned type I jets (FR Is) at lower left.
Our results support the general picture where structured (weak/type I) jets follow largely horizontal movement through the $\nu_\mathrm{peak}-L_\mathrm{peak}$ plane.

why_this_data.value: Collecting the largest possible sample of well-characterized jet SEDs (rather than small statistically complete samples) is best suited to revealing full population characteristics and determining which parts of parameter space are filled or empty.

evidence.quote: We have opted for this approach because it is better suited to revealing the characteristics of the full population, and because looking at the largest possible sample is the best way to answer questions of which parts of the parameter space are filled or empty.

why_this_method.value: Low-frequency (300 MHz) extended radio luminosity (L_ext) is isotropic and correlates with lifetime-integrated jet power, avoiding the Doppler boosting degeneracies that affect radio core luminosity, and can be obtained for over a thousand sources.

evidence.quote: In comparison, the radio core luminosity is not a good indicator of the true jet power, as it is enhanced by orders of magnitude from the intrinsic value due to Doppler boosting, and in general there is a strong degeneracy between angle, speed, and the intrinsic luminosity.

However, it is the only estimate of jet power which we can easily obtain for a large sample (over a thousand sources as noted below), and with appropriate caution it should be suitable for broad characterization of large samples.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Using only statistically complete samples was rejected because such samples are small and almost none have well-constrained broadband SEDs for the entire sample.

evidence.quote: While there are advantages to using only statistically complete samples, there are also major disadvantages – namely, that such samples are small, and almost none have well-constrained broad-band SEDs for the entire sample as we require here.

limitations_admitted.value: Extended radio emission (L_ext) has considerable dispersion around jet power scaling relations and is not reliable for individual sources.

evidence.quote: The extended radio emission is not a perfect measure of jet power, as there is considerable dispersion around the scaling relations referenced above, and it is almost certainly not reliable for individual sources (cite: 2013MNRAS.430..174H).

limitations_admitted.value: About 10% of the TEX sample (103 sources) and 16% of the UEX sample (169 sources) lack redshift measurements and are assigned z=0.3 (though excluded from luminosity plots).

evidence.loc: The TEX and UEX Jet Samples
evidence.quote: In the TEX sample 103 sources (169 in the UEX sample) have no redshift information available on SIMBAD/NED. In these cases a value of $z=0.3$ is assumed ($\approx 10\%$ of the TEX sample, 16% of the UEX sample).

limitations_admitted.value: The Orientation Indicator (OI) definition is not rigorous, could be affected by selection effects, and is meant to be illustrative rather than conclusive.

evidence.quote: We also note that our definition of OI is far from rigorous and could be affected by selection effects, and the use of it here is meant to be more illustrative than conclusive.

limitations_admitted.value: Small number of weak-zone sources with measured black hole masses and L_ext detections (as opposed to upper limits) gives low statistical power to detect an L_ext - M_BH correlation.

evidence.loc: Results and Discussion, Accretion Mode in type I and II Jets
evidence.quote: but the small number of measurements compared to upper limits gives us low statistical power to detect a correlation.

limitations_admitted.value: Misaligned jets (radio galaxies) and low-power jets with well-sampled jet SEDs remain rare, and excitation index was not explicitly accounted for in radio galaxy classifications.

evidence.quote: While we have included as many misaligned jets (i.e., radio galaxies) as possible, those with well-sampled jet SEDs remain rare, as is also the case for low-power jets like those increasingly found in LLAGN (some of which are formally radio-quiet).
Such a study should also explicitly take into account the excitation index.

referee_caveats_inferred: The sample of 2124 sources is a heterogeneous compilation from 23 catalogs with visual SED selection, introducing complex, unmodeled selection biases.
Multi-wavelength SED data compiled from NED and various catalogs are non-simultaneous, which can significantly affect peak frequency and luminosity fits for highly variable blazars.
Visual inspection and hand-selection were used to filter outliers, add Big Blue Bump components, and reject poorly sampled SEDs, making the exact sample selection subjective.

reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: Hundreds of GB to a few TB for raw visibility data of 169 ALMA and 460 VLA/JVLA continuum observations; a few MB for the machine-readable catalog tables.
reproducibility.score_reason: While the final derived catalogs and core flux tables are published as machine-readable supplementary material, reproducing the measurements from raw data to final SEDs is hindered by subjective visual filtering/fitting of 6856 SEDs, unreleased SED/decomposition fitting code, and incomplete imaging/self-calibration parameters for hundreds of radio/mm datasets.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: ALMA plays a minor supporting role (providing single-frequency core continuum fluxes for 169 observations out of a multi-wavelength database of >2000 sources), and the full SED compilation and visual vetting pipeline is not self-contained or automated.

methods_papers.why: Defines the parametric SED model, multivariate KDE method for radio galaxies, visual SED selection procedure, and TEX/UEX sample definitions inherited by this study.
Provides the scaling relation used to convert 300-MHz extended radio luminosity (L_ext) into kinetic jet power (L_kin).
Provides the decelerating relativistic jet flow model used to compute theoretical de-beaming tracks in the nu_peak - L_peak plane.
